findings.title: Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of the dataset actually being queried
findings.body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the helper is invoked with the closure-captured `dataset` (the dataset requested by the client) rather than the function's `scoped_dataset` argument, which is the dataset actually executed against. In `get_event_stats_factory`, widget-splitting can pass a different `split_dataset` (e.g. `discover` when the original requested dataset is `transactions`), and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` then evaluates `dataset == errors/transactions/discover` against the wrong dataset. The result is that upsampling is silently skipped (or wrongly applied) for any query where the requested dataset and the executed dataset differ, including the widget split path. Pass `scoped_dataset` (or both) to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` so the decision is based on the dataset that will actually run.

findings.title: Only the literal token `count()` is rewritten; other common count-style aggregations are silently left as raw counts
findings.body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites columns whose stripped/lowercased form is exactly the string `"count()"`. Any column with arguments (`count_if(...)`, `count_unique(...)`, `count_distinct(...)`), aliased forms (`count() AS total`), whitespace inside the parens (`count(  )`), or counts appearing inside an `equation` expression is left untouched and will be executed against `sample_weight` semantics on some datasets and raw event semantics on others. The docstring says it "transforms aggregation functions to use sum(sample_weight) instead of count()" implying plural coverage; in reality it is a single literal-string match. Either expand the matcher to cover the realistic variants or document the limitation clearly and reject unhandled inputs so callers cannot get silently-mixed semantics.

findings.title: _is_error_focused_query misses queries that target errors by exclusion
findings.body: The check only looks for the substring `event.type:error` in the raw `query` parameter. Common Sentry search syntax that targets errors by negating the transaction type (e.g. `!event.type:transaction`, or `event.type:error OR ...`) is missed — `!event.type:transaction` will return False even though it is an errors-only query, so upsampling is skipped for those queries. Worse, the substring match is naive: a query like `event.type:errorcount` (an unknown tag name in user queries) would also pass. Use the parsed token list from `event_search.parse_search_query` (the same parser the rest of this endpoint uses) and inspect the `event.type` clause's value rather than substring-matching on the raw query string.

findings.title: Upsampling integration tests assert an upsampled value that requires `sample_weight` to be populated by ingest
findings.body: `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10`, deriving that 10 from the stored `client_sample_rate=0.1` and the Snuba `upsampled_count() = sum(sample_weight)` definition in `discover.py`. In `SnubaTestCase` no Relay pipeline runs and `sample_weight` is not populated from the `sample_rate` set by `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling`; `sum(NULL)` over the column will be NULL/0 and the assertion will fail, or — even worse — pass only by accident and silently never validate the upsampling transformation. Either populate `sample_weight` in the test fixture (or wrap the assertion in a mock that returns the expected sample_weight), or split the test so that it verifies (a) the SQL emitted by `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` and (b) the upsampled result via a controlled sample_weight fixture.

findings.title: Integration tests do not invalidate the upsampling eligibility cache, so order-dependent failures are likely
findings.body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` writes `is_eligible` to the shared cache under a key derived only from `organization.id` and the sorted project IDs. The new test class exercises four different allowlist configurations against the same `(organization, [project, project2])` tuple. Without invalidating the cache (e.g. by calling the exposed `invalidate_upsampling_cache` helper or clearing the cache backend in `setUp`/`tearDown`), the first test that runs caches its result and subsequent tests will read that stale value and silently skip the upsampling path they are trying to exercise. Add cache cleanup in `setUp`/`tearDown`, or assert on the emitted SnQL instead of the response value to make the tests order-independent.

findings.title: The main public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` have no direct tests
findings.body: The unit test file only exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. It does not test the actual public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (including its caching behavior, short-circuit when the allowlist is missing, or that it combines the allowlist check with the dataset/query check correctly), nor does it test `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given that the function is the one wired into the request hot-path and contains the non-trivial cache logic flagged in other findings, it deserves direct unit tests.

findings.title: Cache value caches only the allowlist result; the transform check still runs on every cache hit
findings.body: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches only the boolean returned by `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`. On a cache hit the function still executes `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)`, which performs module-identity comparisons, parses the query string, and runs lazy imports of `sentry.snuba.discover/errors/transactions` on every call. To make the 60 s TTL actually pay off, include the relevant decision inputs (or the combined boolean) in the cache value so cache hits short-circuit the full check. At minimum, hoist the `from sentry.snuba import …` statements to module scope so a cache hit is genuinely cheap.

findings.title: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling accepts arbitrary floats including invalid sample rates
findings.body: The helper writes `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever `client_sample_rate` is truthy and converts cleanly. It does not validate the resulting value: 0 (everything dropped → sample_weight = ∞), negative values, or values > 1 are all accepted. A client (or a misbehaving test fixture) can supply `client_sample_rate=0.0` and silently produce divide-by-zero / infinity in the server-side upsampling, or supply `client_sample_rate=-1.0` and corrupt aggregated metrics. Validate the value is in the open interval (0.0, 1.0] before assigning.

findings.title: Overly broad `except Exception: pass` in _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling hides real bugs
findings.body: Two nested `try/except Exception: pass` blocks silently swallow everything, including programming errors like the `normalized_data` object not being a `MutableMapping` at all (e.g. someone refactors `store_event` and passes the wrong value). The first block only needs to handle the case where `contexts` is not a mapping (AttributeError / TypeError), and the second only needs to handle `ValueError` from `float()`. Narrow the exception types so genuine bugs surface instead of being papered over.

findings.title: Repeated in-function imports of sentry.snuba modules on every call
findings.body: `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` does `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` and `from sentry.snuba import transactions` inside the function body, executing those imports on every invocation (including every cache-hit path from `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`). There is no circular-import reason to defer them — `sentry.snuba` does not import this helper. Move the three imports to module top-level so each call is a constant-time identity comparison.
